source.title: Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history from childhood to adolescence to adulthood
source.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

confidence_rationale: Behavioural evidence that the weight given to the already-favoured hypothesis is itself developmentally asymmetric: preschoolers adopt an unfamiliar but better-supported causal hypothesis more readily than older children, adolescents or adults, who cling to the familiar one. That is the human signature of a dominant scorer whose effective weight is low early and grows with age -- the asymmetry ARC-075 wants engineered. Confidence is modest because the data are descriptive (no manipulation of the asymmetry), and because the social domain shows a second flexible period in adolescence, complicating a single open window.
failure_signatures: In the physical domain flexibility declines from preschool to school age to adolescence/adulthood, but in the social domain adolescents are as flexible as preschoolers and more flexible than 6-year-olds and adults -- flexibility is non-monotone and domain-specific, not one early window.
Older learners prefer a familiar hypothesis that is less consistent with the evidence, so the adult default is a prior-dominated monostrategy even when data favour an alternative.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Extended human childhood and adolescence allow a balance between exploration and exploitation and between wider and narrower hypothesis search, with different developmental periods associated with different learning strategies. In two causal-learning studies, preschoolers were better than school-aged children, who were better than adolescents and adults, at learning an unusual physical causal relation; older learners were less likely to adopt an initially unfamiliar hypothesis consistent with new evidence and preferred a familiar, less consistent one. In the social domain preschoolers and adolescents were the most flexible learners.
mapping.ree_translation: The 'familiar hypothesis' plays the role of F's accumulated preference; the 'unusual hypothesis consistent with evidence' is what a diversity circuit would propose. Early in life the familiar hypothesis carries little weight against evidence, so alternatives win easily; later it dominates. ARC-075 asserts REE needs that asymmetry by construction (F's update weight suppressed in the open window), rather than hoping a phase schedule produces it. The adolescent social-domain re-opening is consistent with MECH-335's idea of staggered, domain- or loop-specific windows.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The studies measure hypothesis adoption in short causal-learning tasks, not update magnitudes, and they are cross-sectional age comparisons with no manipulation. Children also simply have weaker priors because they have seen less, so the asymmetry could be an experience effect rather than an actively gated plasticity magnitude -- which is precisely the distinction ARC-075 turns on. The domain-specific, non-monotone pattern means a single infant open window is at best a simplification.
mapping.source_context: Human developmental psychology; cross-sectional causal-learning tasks (physical 'blicket'-style and social) from preschool through adulthood.

confidence_components.notes: Well-regarded group and venue, two studies, but descriptive and cross-sectional. The key confound for ARC-075 -- experience-driven prior strength vs actively gated update magnitude -- is not resolved by this design.
